source.title: Demystifying Verbatim Memorization in Large Language Models
source.authors: Jing Huang; Diyi Yang; Christopher Potts

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates existing unlearning methods against newly designed position and semantic prompt perturbations, reporting extraction outcomes with a different stress-test measure.
record.gate_note: The unlearning stress-test results in Table 2 and the stated 22% to 56% fully extractable-sequence change bear on prompt-only recovery and unlearning robustness. The activation-intervention results in Sections 4.5–4.6 concern memorization mechanisms rather than recovery from unlearning; they are recorded as findings that fit no listed version. The paper does not test fine-tuning recovery or quantization.
record.test_reason: Section 5 applies existing unlearning methods to verbatim-memorized sequences in GPT-Neo 125M. It then measures how much memorized text perturbed prompts still extract. This is a prompt-only recovery test (version E) in a new setting: verbatim memorization rather than hazardous or factual knowledge.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors add that the methods largely prevent generation from the original prefix but do not fully remove the memorized text, which variant prefixes still extract. They also say pruning is more robust but degenerates on perturbed prefixes.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses implementations and setups based on cited gradient-ascent, sparse fine-tuning, and neuron-pruning methods, then evaluates them with position and semantic stress-test prompts. It uses GPT-Neo 125M and a memorized 50-token continuation setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported extraction outcome varies by unlearning method and prompt set. Neuron pruning is described as more robust to stress tests than gradient ascent and sparse fine-tuning, but can degenerate on perturbed prefixes.

fits_no_version.finding: A control model that never saw the sequences predicts about 25% of memorized tokens. Cross-model interventions yield the first 1–2 memorized tokens, and most layers show Ri,1 above 50%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Verbatim-memorized text is partly reconstructed by general language-modeling computation, so it is hard to localize and remove.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The unlearning stress test uses GPT-Neo 125M and a 50-token continuation setup; the reported prompt-perturbation results are max-pooled over around 1K prompts per sequence. The paper does not report a general-ability check for the unlearning evaluation. The authors note neuron pruning can cause degeneration on perturbed prefixes.

untested.parts: Near-chance targeted accuracy is not reported. General-ability retention is not measured for gradient ascent or sparse fine-tuning; the study only cites prior perplexity costs.
Entire version: no relearning fine-tuning attack.
Entire version: no activation-direction ablation on unlearned models. The intervention analyses in Sections 4.5–4.6 are on memorizing models, not unlearned ones.
Jailbreaks, other languages and in-context information are not tested; only position and word-substitution perturbations are.
Entire version: no new robust method is proposed or evaluated as such.

missing.what: Neuron pruning unlearning effect and cost: Δself-accuracy −0.248 and Δneg-accuracy −0.094 on the 90 unlearned sequences
Length-distribution shifts between original and stress-test prompts, per method

record.verdict_notes: The setting is verbatim 50-token memorization in GPT-Neo 125M, not knowledge QA, so near-chance accuracy does not apply directly. Stress-test values are max-pooled over about 1K prompts per sequence, which inflates them relative to single-prompt values. The study is not among the original sources. Relabeled from T2 to T3 because it is a new setting.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests extraction after unlearning and prompt perturbation, but does not establish that targeted-knowledge accuracy is near chance or report a general-ability check.
No post-unlearning relearning fine-tuning attack is tested.
The study does not ablate an activation direction in an unlearned model or analyze whether an unlearning method blocks access rather than deleting information.
No low-bit quantization attack is tested.
The study tests position and semantic prompt perturbations, not jailbreaks, other languages, or in-context information.
Neuron pruning is assessed against position and semantic prompt perturbations, but the study does not test a new method designed to resist fine-tuning, activation-edit, or quantization attacks.

rows.subject: M(∅) with M(X) representations as donor
rows.operation_detail: Cross-model interchange intervention replaces the control model's last-layer residual representations with treatment-model representations.

rows.note: The authors present this result as validating interchangeability of the two models' representations, not as recovery from unlearning.

rows.subject: M(∅) with M(X) representations as donor

relation.reason: The study's own stress tests measure extraction after unlearning.

tranche.reason: New setting (verbatim memorization, GPT-Neo 125M) with a result on recovery by prompt perturbation after unlearning.

source_check.notes: The domain is verbatim-memorized Pile text in GPT-Neo 125M (90 sequences), not hazardous or factual knowledge. Stress-test lengths are max-pooled over about 1K position prompts or about 10 substitutions per word, so they are upper bounds. Some position prompts contain up to 20 continuation tokens. The 22%->56% figure is joint over GA and SFT. The '10-15 tokens' is an average over all three methods; GA/SFT gains are 11-16. Six rows wrongly list the baseline as not stated.

statements.correction: 2407.17817: GPT-Neo 125M, verbatim-memorized 50-token Pile continuations. Gradient ascent: exact-match length 19±18 (original prompt) -> 35±15 (position perturbations; some prompts include up to 20 continuation tokens) and 31±21 (ChatGPT word substitutions). Full 50-token extraction 22% -> 56%, given jointly for gradient ascent and sparse fine-tuning over both perturbation types (R10). Lengths are max-pooled over many prompts.
statements.problem: The study is cited via R2 and R10 but described nowhere. The conditions (forget-query rewrites, TOFU/HP/Senators/multi-hop, 1–32B models) exclude its setting. R2 is position perturbation, and some of those prompts contain continuation tokens, so it is not a pure rewrite.

statements.correction: 2407.17817: neuron pruning on GPT-Neo 125M, exact-match length 4±4 (original prompt) -> 14±8 (position) and 11±10 (semantic). The authors call pruning more robust to the stress tests but note frequent degeneration (repetitive text) on perturbed prefixes. Gradient ascent and sparse fine-tuning recover more (31–36 tokens). So recovery depends on the method but is not absent for pruning.
statements.problem: R8 and R9 show partial recovery under neuron pruning (4 -> 14/11 tokens), not absent recovery. This is limits_scope evidence (the record's own E verdict), not challenges. Neuron pruning and GPT-Neo 125M are missing from the statement's conditions.
No claim about this study and no rows from it. The 2407.15549 named in the statement is a different study.
